item2_roofShading.verdict: RIGHT SIDE UP, at LoD 2 and at LoD 0
item2_roofShading.howTheGBufferWasReached: window has no engine handle, so the live ViewInstance was found by walking the React fiber from the canvas's container (a useRef hook whose .current carries globe/camera/atmosphere). view.buffers reports { normal: true, ... }, so the MRT normal attachment IS allocated in the app's effect set. The MRTPassEffectDesc was found by its normalBuffer getter, its WebGLRenderTarget by textures.includes(tex) (textureIndex 1, HalfFloatType), and the whole attachment was read back with renderer.readRenderTargetPixels and decoded with the engine's own unpackVec2ToNormal (octahedral, jcgt.org/published/0003/02/01).
item2_roofShading.theCaveatThatMatters: The normal G-buffer CANNOT by itself discriminate a flipped winding on this material, and the engine's shader source says why: the MRT write is `vec3 finalNormal = origNormal; GBUFFER_WRITE_NORMAL(finalNormal, reflectivity, roughnessFactor)`, and `origNormal = vec3(normal)` is injected at `#include <normal_fragment_maps>` — DOWNSTREAM of three's `#include <normal_fragment_begin>`, where `normal *= faceDirection` already flipped the normal of a back-facing fragment because createCityMaterial is DoubleSide. So a camera-facing fragment always stores a camera-facing normal. The buffer is therefore evidence that the SHADED normal is right side up; the winding itself is measured by the geometry census below.

gBufferAtLod2.note: 0.003 % of the frame. The cruder 'facing the camera's Z axis' test flags 18,993 (3.6 %), which is an artefact of that test: away from the frame centre the eye ray is not the camera axis, so an off-axis silhouette reads as back-facing by construction. The eye-ray test is the one that means anything.

geometryCensus.what: The per-triangle FLAT face normals in the live scene graph — the `normal` attribute buildCityMeshArrays writes from the winding decision, which is what feeds vNormal and hence the G-buffer, BEFORE the faceDirection flip. Read from the city meshes (MeshLambertMaterial, vertexColors, DoubleSide) by traversing the engine's scene; each mesh's local +Z was confirmed to be world up (500/500 sampled triangles agree with the normalized world position; |worldPos| = 6,371,051 m).

lod2_auto.reading: Roofs point up, ground surfaces point down, walls are vertical — the CityJSON convention. Of the 20,329 down-facing horizontal faces, all but 13 sit in the bottom tenth of their own mesh's height range (the building bases). The 13 exceptions, in two meshes at 51-68 % of their mesh height, are 0.008 % of the triangles and are the kind of face a real LoD 2 building has (a courtyard floor, the underside of an overhang) — no cluster, no whole roof.

lod0_pinned.reading: THIS IS THE CASE 2f62b9e FIXES, and it passes: 16,049 of 16,058 horizontal faces (99.94 %) agree on one direction. PLATEAU's LoD 0 is a terrain-following FOOTPRINT — a ground polygon — whose outward normal points DOWN, which is the direction 2f62b9e's own commit message names ('a box seeded from orthometric z would sit a whole geoid undulation below the geometry and flip every ground polygon up'). What the tight ring box produced instead, per that commit's measured table, was a MIXTURE ('lo -1, hi +1') — the highest polygon of a multi-polygon footprint inverted. There is no such mixture here. (The 'downFacingAboveHalfHeight' counter is meaningless at this rung: the whole mesh spans 1 cm in z, so its z-relative buckets are noise.)

item2_roofShading.lowSunRender: winding-flatness-browser-smoke-yokohama-lowsun.png. Under a 15:30-JST winter sun the roofs read BRIGHT against walls that are bright on the sunward side, dark on the other, and a street-level ground in deep shadow. No roof reads darker than the ground beside it, and there is no inverted crease pattern. Compare the default-sun frame, where a near-overhead sun flattens the term and hides nothing either way.

method: Raw CDP (Node 24 global WebSocket against a headless Chrome on a private --remote-debugging-port), one whole scenario per Chrome process, share hash v3 minted by hand. NOTE for the next run: Page.navigate from the app's URL to the same URL plus '#share=…' is a SAME-DOCUMENT fragment navigation and the app ignores it — the share link must arrive on a full document load (a distinct query string does it).
